lessons.title: Energy balance and a sensible deficit

blocks.markdown:
## The basic sum

Your weight trend follows **energy balance**: the energy you eat against the energy you use. Your **maintenance calories** are the intake at which your weight stays stable. Eat below that and you lose weight; above it and you gain. Training changes what the weight is made of, muscle or fat, more than the sum itself.

## Estimating maintenance

A common estimate multiplies resting energy use (the Mifflin–St Jeor equation) by an activity factor. For most people the estimate is within about 10% of reality, but some are further off. Treat it as a starting point; your weight trend over two to three weeks tells you the real number.

blocks.alt: Three paces of weekly weight loss as a share of body weight: 0.5% gentle, 0.75% steady, 1% fast. Slower paces keep more muscle and strength; above about 1% muscle loss rises.
blocks.caption: How fast to lose

blocks.markdown:
## How fast to lose

A review of evidence for natural lifters suggests losing about 0.5–1% of body weight a week. In a study of athletes, the group losing about 0.7% a week gained lean mass and strength, while the group losing about 1.4% a week did not gain lean mass.

For an 80 kg person, 0.5–1% is 0.4–0.8 kg a week: roughly a 400–900 kcal daily deficit. Most beginners do well starting at the gentle end, about 300–500 kcal a day.

## Before you count anything

If counting food has caused problems for you in the past, or if you are pregnant, under 18 or managing a medical condition, skip the numbers and work with a doctor or registered dietitian. The tracking in Lesson 9.8 also works without calorie counting.

**What this means for your training:** estimate maintenance, aim for a gentle deficit of about 0.5–0.75% of body weight a week, and let your weekly weight trend, not the formula, set the final number.

cards.back: The daily intake at which your weight stays stable. Formulas estimate it within about 10%; your weight trend confirms it.
About 0.5–1% of body weight a week. Slower paces keep more muscle and strength.

questions.stem: You weigh 80 kg and want to keep as much muscle as possible while losing fat. Which weekly pace fits best?
questions.explanation: 0.5–0.75% of 80 kg is 0.4–0.6 kg: the gentle-to-steady end.

questions.stem: Your formula says 2,500 kcal maintenance, but after three weeks at 2,500 your weekly average weight is falling. What's true?
options: Your real maintenance is higher than the estimate
questions.explanation: The trend is the real-world check: stable intake with falling weight means maintenance is higher.

blocks.markdown:

2. **Review** — Helms ER, Aragon AA, Fitschen PJ, Evidence-based recommendations for natural bodybuilding contest preparation: nutrition and supplementation, J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2014;11:20.

lessons.title: Protein: how much, when, from where

blocks.markdown:
## How much

A 2018 meta-analysis of 49 trials found that extra protein added muscle during resistance training, and the benefit plateaued around 1.6 g per kg of body weight a day; some people may benefit up to about 2.2 g/kg. So a practical **protein target** is 1.6–2.2 g/kg a day. In a calorie deficit, aim for the upper half to help protect muscle.

blocks.alt: Protein per typical portion: chicken 100 g ≈ 30 g, skyr 200 g ≈ 20 g, 3 eggs ≈ 18 g, tofu 150 g ≈ 20 g, lentils 150 g cooked ≈ 13 g, whey scoop ≈ 20–25 g.
blocks.caption: Where the protein comes from

blocks.markdown:
## When

Total daily protein matters more than exact timing; a 2013 meta-analysis found timing made little difference once totals were matched. A simple pattern is three to four meals with about 0.4 g/kg each, for example 30–35 g per meal at 80 kg.

## From where

Meat, fish, eggs and dairy are dense in protein. Plant sources such as tofu, tempeh, lentils, beans and seitan work too; mix several over the day. Protein powder is simply food in a convenient form. Values in the picture are approximate and vary by product.

People with kidney disease should agree protein intake with their doctor.

## Try the estimator

The tool below gives ranges for maintenance calories, a target intake and protein. It shows ranges, not prescriptions, and the weekly check tells you how to adjust.

blocks.title: Protein and energy estimator
blocks.description: Enter age, height, weight, activity and goal to see ranges for maintenance, a target intake and daily protein, with a weekly check rule.

blocks.markdown: **What this means for your training:** aim for 1.6–2.2 g of protein per kg a day, split over three or four meals of about 0.4 g/kg; in a deficit, stay in the upper half.

cards.back: About 1.6–2.2 g per kg of body weight a day; the upper half in a calorie deficit.
About 0.4 g/kg per meal over 3–4 meals (about 30–35 g at 80 kg). Totals matter more than timing.

lessons.title: Carbohydrates, fats and eating around training

blocks.markdown:
## Carbohydrates fuel hard work

Carbohydrates are the main fuel for hard efforts such as sprints in sport and hard sets. You don't need special fuelling for a 30-minute strength session: a normal meal one to three hours before is enough. For a 90-minute match, a carbohydrate-rich meal beforehand helps.

## Fats are essential

Fats carry fat-soluble vitamins and support hormones. European reference intakes put fat at 20–35% of energy. In a deficit, cut a little from both carbohydrates and fats rather than removing one completely.

blocks.alt: A plate split into half vegetables, a quarter protein and a quarter starchy carbs, plus a timeline: meal 1–3 h before training, protein-rich meal within a few hours after.
blocks.caption: A simple plate and timing

blocks.markdown:
## Eating around training

- **Before:** a normal meal 1–3 hours earlier, or a small snack if it's been longer.
- **After:** a protein-rich meal within a few hours. The 'anabolic window' is much wider than the 30 minutes often claimed.
- **Every meal (practice):** half the plate vegetables or fruit, a quarter protein, a quarter starchy carbohydrate, plus some fat.
**What this means for your training:** eat normal mixed meals around training: carbs for hard sessions and sport, protein after, and no special timing rules for short strength sessions.

cards.back: The main fuel for hard efforts. A normal meal 1–3 h before is enough for a 30-minute session; more matters for long matches.
About 20–35% of energy (European reference intakes). Don't cut fat to near zero in a deficit.

questions.explanation: After six hours, a small snack helps; no special products needed.

2. **Meta-analysis** — Schoenfeld BJ, Aragon AA, Krieger JW, The effect of protein timing on muscle strength and hypertrophy, J Int Soc Sports Nutr 2013;10:53.
3. **Practice** — training and coaching conventions; labelled as practice in the lesson.
4. **Image** — own diagram.

## Hydration

For most sessions, drinking to thirst is enough. Pale-yellow urine is a simple sign you're well hydrated. In long or hot sport, sports-medicine guidance is to avoid losing more than about 2% of body weight in sweat; weighing yourself before and after a long match shows your losses.

## Alcohol

In a study of trained men, a large dose of alcohol (about 12 drinks) after training cut muscle protein building by about 24%, even when protein was eaten. Smaller amounts haven't been tested as well. Alcohol also adds 7 kcal per gram and disturbs sleep, which makes a deficit harder.

blocks.alt: Three panels: drink to thirst with pale-yellow urine as a check; alcohol after training cut muscle building by about 24% in one study; fibre 25–29 g a day linked with better health.
blocks.caption: Fluids, alcohol and fibre

blocks.markdown:
## Fibre

A 2019 Lancet series found that eating 25–29 g of fibre a day was linked with lower rates of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and death compared with low intakes. Fibre also keeps you full in a deficit. Vegetables, fruit, beans, lentils, oats and wholegrains are the easy sources.
**What this means for your training:** drink to thirst, keep alcohol occasional and away from training days, and build meals around vegetables, beans and wholegrains for about 25–29 g of fibre a day.

cards.back: Drink to thirst; pale-yellow urine. In long, hot sport, avoid losing more than about 2% of body weight.
About 25–29 g a day, linked with lower heart disease, type 2 diabetes and mortality (2019 Lancet).

questions.explanation: A large dose after training reduced muscle building.

questions.explanation: Wholegrains, beans, vegetables and fruit add fibre.

lessons.title: Supplements: what works and what doesn't

blocks.markdown:
## Worth considering

- **Creatine monohydrate:** the best-researched supplement for strength training. 3–5 g a day adds small extra gains in strength and lean mass; no loading phase is needed. Expect 1–2 kg of extra water weight at first.
- **Caffeine:** 3–6 mg per kg about an hour before training can improve performance. Coffee works.
- **Protein powder:** convenient food, not magic.

blocks.alt: Three tiers: good evidence (creatine, caffeine, protein powder as food), only if low (vitamin D), not needed (fat burners, BCAAs with enough protein, testosterone boosters).
blocks.caption: Supplement evidence tiers

blocks.markdown:
## Only if you need it

**Vitamin D** helps if your levels are low, which is common in northern winters. A blood test or a talk with your doctor decides; it isn't a performance booster otherwise.

## Not needed

Fat burners, testosterone boosters and BCAAs (if you already eat enough protein) add cost without clear benefit. Supplements can also be contaminated; if you buy any, choose products tested by an independent programme. Check with a doctor before supplements if you take medicines or have kidney disease.

**What this means for your training:** food, training and sleep come first. If you add anything, creatine monohydrate at 3–5 g a day and your usual coffee before training are the best-supported choices.

cards.back: 3–5 g a day; small extra gains in strength and lean mass. No loading needed; 1–2 kg water weight at first.
About 3–6 mg/kg about an hour before training. Late doses can cost sleep.

lessons.title: Sleep and stress: the recovery you can't buy

blocks.markdown:
## How much sleep

Sleep experts recommend 7–9 hours a night for adults. Muscle repair, hormone balance and appetite control all depend on it.

## Sleep and fat loss

In a controlled study, adults on the same calorie deficit slept either 8.5 or 5.5 hours a night for 14 days. With 8.5 hours they lost 1.4 kg of fat and 1.5 kg of fat-free mass. With 5.5 hours they lost only 0.6 kg of fat and 2.4 kg of fat-free mass: much more of the loss came from muscle and other lean tissue.

blocks.alt: Bars from a 14-day deficit study: with 8.5 h sleep, 1.4 kg fat and 1.5 kg fat-free mass lost; with 5.5 h sleep, 0.6 kg fat and 2.4 kg fat-free mass lost.
blocks.caption: Short sleep, less fat lost

blocks.markdown:
## Habits that help

- Keep regular sleep and wake times.
- Stop caffeine well before bed: 400 mg taken even 6 hours before bed cut sleep by more than an hour in one study.
- Keep the bedroom dark and cool.

## Stress counts too

Work stress, travel and family pressure use the same recovery budget. In heavy weeks, cut a set per exercise or take the deload from Module 6 early.
**What this means for your training:** protect 7–9 hours of sleep, especially in a deficit. On short-sleep or high-stress weeks, train lighter rather than skipping or grinding through.

cards.back: 7–9 hours a night for adults. Short sleep in a deficit shifts loss from fat towards lean mass.
A large dose even 6 hours before bed cut sleep by over an hour in one study. Keep coffee to earlier in the day.

questions.stem: In the 14-day deficit study, what happened with 5.5 hours of sleep?
options: Less fat and more fat-free mass were lost
questions.explanation: 0.6 kg fat and 2.4 kg fat-free mass, against 1.4 and 1.5 kg with 8.5 hours.

questions.stem: You've slept 5 hours for three nights during a heavy work week. What's the best training choice?
options: Train lighter, e.g. one fewer set per exercise
questions.explanation: Stress uses the same recovery budget.

lessons.title: Soreness, pain or injury: train, adapt or stop

blocks.markdown:
## Normal soreness

**Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS)** usually peaks one to three days after new or harder exercise and fades as you get used to it. You can train through mild soreness with lighter loads; it isn't a sign of a good or bad session.

blocks.alt: Traffic light for pain during exercise on a 0–10 scale: green 0–2 continue, amber 3–5 adapt if it settles by the next morning, red above 5 or worse next day stop that exercise.
blocks.caption: A pain traffic light

blocks.markdown:
## A pain traffic light

This approach comes from a tendon-rehabilitation study and is used widely in practice:

- **Green (0–2 out of 10):** continue.
- **Amber (3–5):** acceptable if it settles by the next morning and isn't getting worse week to week. Reduce load, range or change the exercise.
- **Red (above 5, or worse the next day):** stop that exercise and use a pain-free alternative. If it doesn't improve within a week or two, see a physiotherapist or doctor.

## Stop and get help now

**Red-flag symptoms** need medical attention, not training adjustments:

- chest pain or pressure, fainting, or unusual breathlessness: stop and call emergency services
- a sudden sharp pain, a 'pop', rapid swelling or a joint giving way
- numbness, tingling or weakness spreading into a limb
- pain at night or at rest that keeps getting worse

This course doesn't diagnose injuries; when in doubt, ask a professional.
**What this means for your training:** rate pain during and after sessions. Green: continue. Amber: adapt and watch the next morning. Red or red-flag symptoms: stop and get it checked.

cards.back: Delayed-onset muscle soreness: peaks 1–3 days after new or harder exercise. Train lighter through it; it fades with practice.
0–2 continue; 3–5 adapt if it settles by next morning; above 5 or worse next day, stop that exercise.

2. **Tool** — PAR-Q+ (2023 version), the Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire for Everyone (Module 0).
3. **Practice** — training and coaching conventions; labelled as practice in the lesson.

## Why the scale lies day to day

Body weight can swing 1–2 kg from one day to the next with water, salt, carbohydrate, gut contents and, at first, creatine. Weigh yourself on waking, after the toilet, three or more times a week, and compare **weekly averages**, not single days.

blocks.alt: A zigzag line of daily weights over four weeks with a smooth line of 7-day averages falling steadily by about 0.5 kg a week.
blocks.caption: Daily noise, weekly trend

blocks.markdown:
## Four measures together

- **Weight trend:** weekly average.
- **Waist:** at the navel, relaxed, same time of day, every two weeks.
- **Photos:** monthly, same light, same pose.
- **Strength:** your log. Strength rising while weight falls means you're keeping muscle.

## Adjusting (practice)

- Losing less than about 0.25% a week for 2–3 weeks: cut about 100–200 kcal a day or add 2,000 daily steps.
- Losing more than 1% a week, or strength falling: eat a little more.
- Waist down and strength up at stable weight: recomposition is working; keep going.

If tracking starts to feel stressful or obsessive, drop the numbers and use photos, waist and strength, or talk to a professional.
**What this means for your training:** log a weekly average weight, waist every two weeks, monthly photos and your strength numbers. Adjust intake only after two to three weeks of the same trend.

cards.back: Mean of several morning weigh-ins. Daily swings of 1–2 kg are mostly water and food.
At the navel, relaxed, same time of day, every two weeks. Falls with fat loss even when weight stalls.
